findings.title: Raw, unhashed recovery codes are handed to user storage while the read path expects hashed credential data
findings.body: createRecoveryCodesCredential serializes the plain `generatedCodes` list with `JsonSerialization.writeValueAsString(generatedCodes)` and passes it to `user.credentialManager().updateCredential(...)`, whereas the local branch stores `credentialModel`, whose credentialData is the hashed `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialData` produced by `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues`. The read paths (`RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential` followed by `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromCredentialModel` in RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean and RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator) assume the stored credentialData is that hashed object. A user storage provider that persists the value it receives and returns it in a `CredentialModel` (the normal credential-store contract) will (a) keep the recovery codes in plaintext, so compromising the user store directly yields usable login codes, and (b) cause `createFromCredentialModel` to fail deserializing a JSON array into `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialData`, breaking the login form. The bundled BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage only avoids this because its `getCredentials` re-hashes the raw codes itself.

findings.title: Exhausted recovery-code credential in user storage is never removed and can break the next login
findings.body: After a successful code validation, when the credential reports `allCodesUsed()` the code calls `authenticatedUser.credentialManager().removeStoredCredentialById(...)`. That method only operates on Keycloak's local credential store; now that recovery-code credentials may live in a user storage provider, a federated credential is not removed (and its id is provider-generated, not a local id). If a provider reports all codes used, the credential and `isConfiguredFor(type)` remain true, so the next login selects the recovery-code authenticator and `RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean` calls `getNextRecoveryAuthnCode().get()` on an empty Optional, throwing NoSuchElementException (HTTP 500); at best the stale credential is left behind. Removal should be done through the credential manager's type-based disable or the user storage provider.

findings.title: getCredentials dereferences a possibly null MyUser
findings.body: `getCredentials` does `var myUser = getMyUser(user)` and then dereferences `myUser.recoveryCodes`, unlike `isValid` (line 285) which returns false when the user is not present in this provider. If `getCredentials` is invoked for a user that is not backed by this provider (for example a local user when the provider is enabled in the realm), it throws NullPointerException. Add a `myUser == null` guard returning `Stream.empty()`.

findings.title: No coverage for local fallback or single-use behavior of user-storage recovery codes
findings.body: The new test only covers the case where the user storage advertises and stores recovery codes. There is no test that recovery codes still end up in local storage when the user storage does not support the type (the other branch of createRecoveryCodesCredential), nor that a user-storage-backed recovery code stops working after use. The bundled provider's `isValid` compares the raw code without marking it used and `getCredentials` always rebuilds the model with all codes unused, so the replay-prevention behavior of the new user-storage path is untested.
